screens.title: SSH: purpose and client-server model
screens.narratorSegment: SSH is a cryptographic protocol that creates an encrypted channel between two machines so you can administer a remote system without exposing credentials or commands to the network. The model is simple: your local machine runs an SSH client to initiate a connection, and the remote machine runs the sshd daemon to accept and authenticate that connection. Encryption defends against eavesdropping; authentication ensures the remote server is talking to a trusted client. A concrete example is running a command on a VPS at 203.0.113.5: you type a single ssh command and the terminal becomes a secure remote shell. A common misconception is that SSH only secures passwords; in reality it protects the entire session, including file transfers and remote command outputs. Another important detail is the default port: SSH listens on TCP 22, but you can change it for operational reasons — this does not increase cryptographic strength, it lowers noisy scans. Before changing a port, update your firewall and test an alternate session to avoid lockout. To confirm understanding, try listing the sshd service status and observe where it listens; this connects the protocol idea to a real system view. What would you check first if a remote machine refuses SSH connections?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: SSH provides an encrypted, authenticated channel for remote command execution and file transfer; client and server roles are distinct and critical.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › SSH: purpose and client-server model
Core Concept

SSH protects remote sessions

SSH encrypts both authentication and all subsequent traffic. This means commands, passwords, and file transfers are shielded from eavesdroppers.

  • Client: initiates connections, presents keys or passwords.
  • Server (sshd): listens on port 22 by default and authenticates clients.
  • Encryption prevents passive interception; authentication prevents impersonation.
Key Takeaway

Think of SSH as both a locked tunnel and an identity check for the machines using it.

Example: open a secure shell to a host and run remote commands as if you were there.
# connect to a remote host
ssh cohortia_admin@192.168.1.100
# check sshd status on the remote machine
sudo systemctl status sshd
Common mistake
Assuming changing the SSH port makes the connection cryptographically stronger; it only reduces noise from automated scans.
Check
If a connection fails, verify network reachability, firewall rules, and sshd is running on the expected port.

screens.title: Connecting with the ssh client
screens.narratorSegment: Connecting with the ssh client is often the first practical step you'll take. The simplest invocation supplies a username and a host: ssh username@remote_host. If your local username matches the remote account, you can omit the username and just use the host. When you run that command the client negotiates encryption, authenticates the server, and then prompts for credentials or tries your keys. A concrete example: ssh cohortia_admin@192.168.1.100 will prompt for cohortia_admin’s password unless a matching key is available. You can also specify a nonstandard port with -p or -P depending on the tool; remember scp uses uppercase -P for ports. A common misconception is that repeated failed attempts mean the server is down; often it's a firewall or wrong port. Debugging tips include adding -v to the ssh command to show verbose negotiation steps, and opening a separate console to confirm the server's sshd is running. Practice connecting, then run a few harmless commands such as whoami or uptime to validate your session. Close the session by typing exit. What does the verbose output tell you about authentication failures?

Process

Basic connection patterns

With username

Omitting username (same account)

Verbose debugging

Example and verification

Connect and run a simple check to confirm a usable session.

screens.title: SSH client configuration (~/.ssh/config)
screens.narratorSegment: The ~/. ssh/config file is your personal client configuration and can contain per-host blocks and global settings. A host block lets you create a short alias and define Hostname, User, Port, IdentityFile, and options like ForwardAgent or ServerAliveInterval. For example, adding a Host myserver entry with Hostname 192.168.1.100 and IdentityFile ~/. ssh/id_rsa_myserver lets you type ssh myserver instead of a long command. Global sections like Host * allow you to set keepalive intervals to prevent session timeouts. A helpful concrete step is to create a config and test it immediately: save the file with correct permissions, then run ssh myserver -v to observe how the client applies settings. A common mistake is storing private keys in insecure locations or giving ~/. ssh/config incorrect permissions; the file should be readable only by your user. Another pitfall is forgetting IdentityFile paths are expanded relative to your home directory. After creating a config alias, practice connecting and confirm which key the client offers in a verbose run. How might ServerAliveInterval help when your SSH session stalls behind a NAT? SSH client configuration (~/.ssh/config) means use ~/.ssh/config to simplify connections with aliases and to specify identity files, ports, and global keepalives.. In practical terms, create aliases, set identity files, and global options. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use ~/.ssh/config to simplify connections with aliases and to specify identity files, ports, and global keepalives.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › SSH client configuration
Definition

A single file to manage connections

~/.ssh/config stores Host blocks and global options so repeated flags are unnecessary.

Host myserver
    Hostname 192.168.1.100
    User cohortia_admin
    Port 22
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_rsa_myserver
    ForwardAgent yes

Host *
    ServerAliveInterval 60

Concrete checks

  • Ensure ~/.ssh/config permissions are 600 or 644 depending on distro policy.
  • Run ssh -v myserver to verify the correct identity file is offered.
  • Use Host * for ServerAliveInterval to reduce idle disconnects behind NAT.
Mnemonic
Think: Host alias maps to full connection settings like a contact card.
Pitfall
Incorrect IdentityFile paths or wrong file permissions prevent key usage.

screens.title: Public-key authentication explained
screens.narratorSegment: Public‑key authentication uses a cryptographic pair: a private key that stays on your machine and a public key placed on the remote server in ~/. ssh/authorized_keys. When you connect, the server looks for your public key and then issues a challenge that only the holder of the matching private key can answer. This prevents attackers who know a password from impersonating the key owner, because possession of the private key is required. Generate a key pair with ssh-keygen and protect the private key with a passphrase; the passphrase protects your private key if the file is stolen. A concrete example is running ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 to create a strong RSA pair, then copying the. pub file to the server. A common misconception is that keys are magic — they still require safe storage, correct permissions, and careful distribution. If ~/. ssh/authorized_keys has loose permissions the server will ignore keys. After installing a public key, test login and keep a password-capable session open until you confirm the key works. How would you recover access if you accidentally removed all keys and disabled password authentication?

keyIdea.title: Authentication
keyIdea.text: Public-key authentication proves identity by cryptographic challenge-response and removes the need for typing passwords when properly set up.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Public-key authentication explained
Core Concept

Keys prove identity without passwords

The server holds your public key and challenges your client to prove possession of the private key when you attempt to authenticate.

# generate a key pair (local machine)
ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "your_email@example.com"
# public key file: ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub
# private key file: ~/.ssh/id_rsa (protect this file)
Concrete example: after generating keys, append the public key to the remote file ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and test that ssh logs you in without a password. Keep a separate open connection until keys are confirmed.
Security note
Always protect your private key with a passphrase or use ssh-agent to cache it temporarily during your session.
Common mistake
Loose permissions on ~/.ssh or authorized_keys cause the server to ignore keys; ensure restrictive modes.

screens.title: Generate SSH key pairs (ssh-keygen)
screens.narratorSegment: Generating an SSH key pair is a simple, repeatable task. Use ssh-keygen with an algorithm and key length you trust, for example ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "your_email@example. com". The command creates a private key and a public key file in ~/. ssh. When prompted for a passphrase, prefer to set one: it encrypts your private key on disk and prevents immediate use if the file is stolen. If you need automation, a passphrase-less key can be acceptable for short‑lived service accounts, but balance convenience and risk. After generation, check the files and set strict permissions: private key at 600 and ~/. ssh at 700. A concrete example: run ssh-keygen interactively, then inspect permissions with ls -la ~/. ssh. A common misconception is believing only the public key needs protection; while it is safe to share, its integrity matters, and the private key must remain secret. As a final step, test the key locally with ssh -i ~/. ssh/id_rsa user@host and ensure the server accepts the public key. Consider using ssh-agent to avoid entering your passphrase every time while preserving the additional security it provides.

keyIdea.title: Key Generation
keyIdea.text: Choose a strong algorithm and key length, protect private keys with a passphrase, and set strict filesystem permissions on keys and ~/.ssh.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Generate SSH key pairs
Process

Run ssh-keygen and protect keys

ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "your_email@example.com"
# follow prompts to save files and set a passphrase
# verify files:
ls -la ~/.ssh/id_rsa ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub
After creation, set permissions: chmod 700 ~/.ssh and chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_rsa. These modes ensure SSH will accept the private key for authentication.

Example decision

Use a passphrase for interactive user keys. For automation, consider a dedicated key stored safely and limited by server-side authorized_keys options.

Pro tip
Add keys to ssh-agent with ssh-add to cache the decrypted key for your session and avoid repeated passphrase prompts.
Mistake
Storing private keys on shared or unsecured storage risks credential theft; keep them in your home ~/.ssh only.

screens.title: Copying the public key to a server
screens.narratorSegment: After generating a key pair, the next step is placing the public key on the remote server. The easiest tool is ssh-copy-id which logs in with your password, creates ~/. ssh if needed, and appends your public key to ~/. ssh/authorized_keys with correct permissions. For example: ssh-copy-id username@remote_host_ip. If ssh-copy-id is unavailable, you can manually append the public key by piping it over SSH and ensuring directories and file modes are correct. A concrete manual command is: cat ~/. ssh/id_rsa. pub | ssh username@remote_host_ip "mkdir -p ~/. ssh && chmod 700 ~/. ssh && cat >> ~/. ssh/authorized_keys && chmod 600 ~/. ssh/authorized_keys". A common misconception is that simply copying the text is enough; permissions and ownership on the server side must be strict for sshd to accept the key. After copying, test login from a fresh terminal so you replicate a first login. If you cannot log in with the key, check server-side authorized_keys, ownership, and sshd logs via journalctl. Always keep an active session until you verify key-based access to avoid lockout. Copying the public key to a server means prefer ssh-copy-id for convenience; manual copy must create ~/.ssh, append the public key, and set strict permissions to succeed.. In practical terms, use ssh-copy-id or a manual method to populate authorized_keys. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Copying the public key to a server
Process Flow

Automated and manual copy methods

Automatic:
ssh-copy-id username@remote_host_ip
Manual (single-line):
cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub | ssh username@remote_host_ip "mkdir -p ~/.ssh && chmod 700 ~/.ssh && cat >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys && chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys"
Concrete check: after the copy, in a new terminal run ssh username@remote_host_ip and confirm no password prompt appears. If it still prompts, inspect permissions and ownership on the remote ~/.ssh and authorized_keys files, and consult sudo journalctl -u sshd for rejection messages.
Why it matters
Automated tools handle permissions for you; manual steps must replicate those changes exactly.
Common mistake
Using incorrect file modes will cause sshd to ignore authorized_keys and fall back to password auth or deny access.

screens.title: Testing keys, passphrases, and ssh-agent
screens.narratorSegment: Once your public key is on the server, test key-based authentication from a new terminal to replicate a first-time login. If you set a passphrase for your private key, ssh will request it; to avoid typing it repeatedly use ssh-agent. Start the agent on your local machine, then add the private key with ssh-add and enter the passphrase once per session. A concrete workflow: ssh-add ~/. ssh/id_rsa, then ssh user@host and you should connect without an interactive passphrase prompt. A common misconception is that ssh-agent weakens security; in reality it preserves the benefit of a passphrase while reducing typing for interactive sessions. Troubleshooting steps include running ssh -v to see which keys were tried and confirming that the private key file permissions are 600. If the agent isn't offering the key, list keys with ssh-add -l and re-add as required. Remember to lock or clear the agent when leaving untrusted environments. Validate and manage keys

Security practice

screens.title: Securing the SSH server (sshd_config)
screens.narratorSegment: The SSH server is configured in /etc/ssh/sshd_config and small changes there have outsized security impact. Key recommended settings include disabling PasswordAuthentication after your key-based logins work, setting PermitRootLogin no to block direct root sessions, and using AllowUsers or AllowGroups to limit who can connect. Changing Port from 22 to another number can reduce automated scanning noise, but it is defense by obscurity and not a substitute for proper authentication. After changing sshd_config you must restart the sshd service with sudo systemctl restart sshd for changes to take effect. A concrete example: to require keys only, set PasswordAuthentication no, then keep an active session while testing a key-based login from a new terminal. A frequent mistake is restarting sshd without updating firewall rules to allow the new port; doing this can lock you out. Also check sshd logs via sudo journalctl -u sshd if keys are rejected — logs often give permission or syntax hints. When you make changes, always verify from another connection and keep a recovery plan like console access or a second SSH session. Securing the SSH server (sshd_config) means edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config to disable passwords and root login, restrict users, and always test changes safely before closing your working session.. Definition

Key sshd_config directives

Port 2222
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
AllowUsers user1 user2
Concrete safeguard: update firewall to allow the chosen port before restarting sshd. Keep one session open while testing changes from a second terminal so you can recover if something goes wrong.
Warning

Check
Restart with sudo systemctl restart sshd and then verify with sudo systemctl status sshd and journalctl -u sshd for errors.

screens.title: Changing SSH port and firewall safety
screens.narratorSegment: Changing the SSH listening port can reduce background scanning noise, but it creates a two‑step operational task: update firewall rules and then update sshd_config. The safe sequence is: open the new port in your firewall first, test connecting to the new port from a separate terminal, and only then restart sshd. For example, open TCP 2222 using your firewall tool, then try ssh -p 2222 user@host from a different console. If the test succeeds, restart sshd and then close the old port. If the test fails, you still have your original session and can revert. A common failure is forgetting to adjust firewall rules, which leads to immediate loss of remote access after restart. Use tools like sudo firewall-cmd --add-port=2222/tcp --permanent and sudo firewall-cmd --reload, or iptables rules depending on your environment. Always leave a recovery path such as console access or an out-of-band console. After the change, update your ~/. ssh/config to include the new port under Host entries so you won't need -p each time. What recovery options would you keep available when making network-critical changes? Process Flow

Safe sequence to change port

  1. 1. Open new port in firewall and keep current port open.
  2. 2. Test connecting to the new port from a separate terminal.

screens.title: Secure file transfer with scp
screens.narratorSegment: scp provides a familiar copy-like interface to transfer files over an SSH connection. Use scp source destination and scp will securely move data while reusing SSH authentication. For example, to copy a local file to a remote /tmp directory: scp /path/to/local/file. txt username@remote_host_ip:/tmp/. To retrieve a file from a remote host, reverse the order: scp username@remote_host_ip:/path/to/remote/file. txt /path/to/local/. For recursive directory copies use -r. If the server listens on a non‑standard port, include -P 2222 (uppercase P). A common mistake is confusing scp’s -P with ssh’s -p; scp uses -P. Also remember that scp will prompt for a password unless you have key-based authentication or an ssh-agent offering keys. A concrete use-case: create a test file locally, scp it to /tmp on the remote host, and then verify it exists with a remote ls command. Note that scp uses SSH under the hood, so firewall and authentication considerations are the same. How would you copy an entire project directory to a remote host preserving its structure? Secure file transfer with scp means scp moves files securely over ssh; use -r for directories and -p to specify a nonstandard port when necessary.. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Secure file transfer with scp
Comparison

scp patterns

Copy local to remote
scp /path/to/local/file.txt username@remote_host_ip:/tmp/
Copy remote to local
scp username@remote_host_ip:/path/to/remote/file.txt /path/to/local/
Recursive directory copy
scp -r /path/to/local/dir username@remote_host_ip:/path/to/remote/
Example port usage: scp -P 2222 file.txt username@remote_host_ip:/tmp/. Remember scp’s -P is uppercase, unlike ssh’s -p. After transfer, verify the file exists remotely using a remote ssh command or sftp session.
Why it matters
scp is a quick, secure way to move files during administration tasks when encryption is required.
Pitfall
Using the wrong port option (-p vs -P) will fail; remember scp uses -P for port numbers.

screens.title: Using sftp and troubleshooting common SSH mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: sftp opens an interactive file transfer session over SSH and behaves similarly to FTP but within an encrypted channel. Start it with sftp username@remote_host_ip and then use commands like ls, cd, get, and put to navigate and transfer files. This is handy when you want an interactive session to inspect remote directories before copying. For scripted single-file transfers, scp is often quicker. Troubleshooting SSH issues usually follows a short checklist: verify sshd is running with sudo systemctl status sshd, inspect logs with sudo journalctl -u sshd, confirm firewall rules allow the port, and check file permissions on ~/. ssh, authorized_keys (should be 600), and private keys (should be 600 or 400). A common exam-style problem is being prompted for a password despite installing a public key; the likely culprit is improper permissions on the private key or on remote ~/. ssh files. The hands-on exercise walks through generating a key, copying it, testing passwordless login, adding a config entry, transferring a file to /tmp with scp, and verifying the file remotely. If you get stuck, which of the checks would you run first and why?

Definition

Interactive file transfer

sftp username@remote_host_ip
# then inside sftp:

Troubleshooting checklist

fullNarratorScript:
SSH is the standard way administrators access Linux servers remotely because it creates an encrypted channel over an untrusted network. In this lesson you will learn the client‑server model behind SSH, practical connection commands, how to set up safer, passwordless logins with public‑key authentication, and secure file transfer with scp and sftp. You will also learn how to harden the SSH daemon on servers to reduce the attack surface and avoid common lockout mistakes. For example, generating a key pair and using ssh-copy-id saves repeated password entry while improving security. You will practice creating a ~/. ssh/config entry to connect with a short alias, and you will see why file permissions and firewall adjustments matter when moving the default SSH port. Throughout, I will show concrete commands you can run in a terminal, common pitfalls to avoid, and simple checks to verify success. By the end, you will be able to authenticate with keys, transfer files securely, and apply a small set of server-side hardening changes without losing access. Ready to begin configuring and testing SSH with safe habits in mind?

These objectives set clear, practical goals. First, you will explain why SSH is the preferred channel for remote administration and what protections encryption and authentication provide. That understanding helps you choose when to use SSH instead of unsecured tools. Second, you will connect to remote systems using the ssh client, including specifying user and host or using a short hostname alias. Practicing the basic connection command lets you validate network reachability and login credentials. Third, you will configure the SSH client with a ~/. ssh/config file so common hosts use aliases, specific keys, or non‑standard ports. Knowing how to author a config entry saves time and reduces typing mistakes. Fourth, you will set up public‑key authentication so you can log in without entering a password each time while improving security. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify your progress: demonstrate a working ssh login, create a key pair, and add a config alias that shortens your connection command. These skills are foundational and will be reinforced with hands‑on steps and common troubleshooting tips throughout the lesson.

These additional objectives cover security, transfer, and troubleshooting. First, you will secure the SSH server by editing /etc/ssh/sshd_config to disable root login, require keys, and optionally change the listening port. Understanding these settings helps you reduce automated attacks and enforce least privilege. Second, you will use scp to copy files and directories over SSH, and sftp for interactive transfers, including examples that specify ports and recursive copy. Third, you will learn to troubleshoot common permission and service problems, such as incorrect file modes on ~/. ssh or a stopped sshd service, and use status commands to diagnose issues. Finally, you will practice safe change procedures: update firewall rules and test connections from a spare terminal before restarting sshd to avoid lockout. Each objective includes a clear verification step so you can confirm competency by performing a passwordless login, transferring a file to /tmp, and restarting sshd without losing access.

SSH is a cryptographic protocol that creates an encrypted channel between two machines so you can administer a remote system without exposing credentials or commands to the network. The model is simple: your local machine runs an SSH client to initiate a connection, and the remote machine runs the sshd daemon to accept and authenticate that connection. Encryption defends against eavesdropping; authentication ensures the remote server is talking to a trusted client. A concrete example is running a command on a VPS at 203.0.113.5: you type a single ssh command and the terminal becomes a secure remote shell. A common misconception is that SSH only secures passwords; in reality it protects the entire session, including file transfers and remote command outputs. Another important detail is the default port: SSH listens on TCP 22, but you can change it for operational reasons — this does not increase cryptographic strength, it lowers noisy scans. Before changing a port, update your firewall and test an alternate session to avoid lockout. To confirm understanding, try listing the sshd service status and observe where it listens; this connects the protocol idea to a real system view. What would you check first if a remote machine refuses SSH connections?

Connecting with the ssh client is often the first practical step you'll take. The simplest invocation supplies a username and a host: ssh username@remote_host. If your local username matches the remote account, you can omit the username and just use the host. When you run that command the client negotiates encryption, authenticates the server, and then prompts for credentials or tries your keys. A concrete example: ssh cohortia_admin@192.168.1.100 will prompt for cohortia_admin’s password unless a matching key is available. You can also specify a nonstandard port with -p or -P depending on the tool; remember scp uses uppercase -P for ports. A common misconception is that repeated failed attempts mean the server is down; often it's a firewall or wrong port. Debugging tips include adding -v to the ssh command to show verbose negotiation steps, and opening a separate console to confirm the server's sshd is running. Practice connecting, then run a few harmless commands such as whoami or uptime to validate your session. Close the session by typing exit. What does the verbose output tell you about authentication failures?

The ~/. ssh/config file is your personal client configuration and can contain per-host blocks and global settings. A host block lets you create a short alias and define Hostname, User, Port, IdentityFile, and options like ForwardAgent or ServerAliveInterval. For example, adding a Host myserver entry with Hostname 192.168.1.100 and IdentityFile ~/. ssh/id_rsa_myserver lets you type ssh myserver instead of a long command. Global sections like Host * allow you to set keepalive intervals to prevent session timeouts. A helpful concrete step is to create a config and test it immediately: save the file with correct permissions, then run ssh myserver -v to observe how the client applies settings. A common mistake is storing private keys in insecure locations or giving ~/. ssh/config incorrect permissions; the file should be readable only by your user. Another pitfall is forgetting IdentityFile paths are expanded relative to your home directory. After creating a config alias, practice connecting and confirm which key the client offers in a verbose run. How might ServerAliveInterval help when your SSH session stalls behind a NAT? SSH client configuration (~/.ssh/config) means use ~/.ssh/config to simplify connections with aliases and to specify identity files, ports, and global keepalives.. In practical terms, create aliases, set identity files, and global options. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Public‑key authentication uses a cryptographic pair: a private key that stays on your machine and a public key placed on the remote server in ~/. ssh/authorized_keys. When you connect, the server looks for your public key and then issues a challenge that only the holder of the matching private key can answer. This prevents attackers who know a password from impersonating the key owner, because possession of the private key is required. Generate a key pair with ssh-keygen and protect the private key with a passphrase; the passphrase protects your private key if the file is stolen. A concrete example is running ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 to create a strong RSA pair, then copying the. pub file to the server. A common misconception is that keys are magic — they still require safe storage, correct permissions, and careful distribution. If ~/. ssh/authorized_keys has loose permissions the server will ignore keys. After installing a public key, test login and keep a password-capable session open until you confirm the key works. How would you recover access if you accidentally removed all keys and disabled password authentication?

Generating an SSH key pair is a simple, repeatable task. Use ssh-keygen with an algorithm and key length you trust, for example ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "your_email@example. com". The command creates a private key and a public key file in ~/. ssh. When prompted for a passphrase, prefer to set one: it encrypts your private key on disk and prevents immediate use if the file is stolen. If you need automation, a passphrase-less key can be acceptable for short‑lived service accounts, but balance convenience and risk. After generation, check the files and set strict permissions: private key at 600 and ~/. ssh at 700. A concrete example: run ssh-keygen interactively, then inspect permissions with ls -la ~/. ssh. A common misconception is believing only the public key needs protection; while it is safe to share, its integrity matters, and the private key must remain secret. As a final step, test the key locally with ssh -i ~/. ssh/id_rsa user@host and ensure the server accepts the public key. Consider using ssh-agent to avoid entering your passphrase every time while preserving the additional security it provides.

After generating a key pair, the next step is placing the public key on the remote server. The easiest tool is ssh-copy-id which logs in with your password, creates ~/. ssh if needed, and appends your public key to ~/. ssh/authorized_keys with correct permissions. For example: ssh-copy-id username@remote_host_ip. If ssh-copy-id is unavailable, you can manually append the public key by piping it over SSH and ensuring directories and file modes are correct. A concrete manual command is: cat ~/. ssh/id_rsa. pub | ssh username@remote_host_ip "mkdir -p ~/. ssh && chmod 700 ~/. ssh && cat >> ~/. ssh/authorized_keys && chmod 600 ~/. ssh/authorized_keys". A common misconception is that simply copying the text is enough; permissions and ownership on the server side must be strict for sshd to accept the key. After copying, test login from a fresh terminal so you replicate a first login. If you cannot log in with the key, check server-side authorized_keys, ownership, and sshd logs via journalctl. Always keep an active session until you verify key-based access to avoid lockout. Copying the public key to a server means prefer ssh-copy-id for convenience; manual copy must create ~/.ssh, append the public key, and set strict permissions to succeed.. Once your public key is on the server, test key-based authentication from a new terminal to replicate a first-time login. If you set a passphrase for your private key, ssh will request it; to avoid typing it repeatedly use ssh-agent. Start the agent on your local machine, then add the private key with ssh-add and enter the passphrase once per session. A concrete workflow: ssh-add ~/. ssh/id_rsa, then ssh user@host and you should connect without an interactive passphrase prompt. A common misconception is that ssh-agent weakens security; in reality it preserves the benefit of a passphrase while reducing typing for interactive sessions. Troubleshooting steps include running ssh -v to see which keys were tried and confirming that the private key file permissions are 600. If the agent isn't offering the key, list keys with ssh-add -l and re-add as required. Remember to lock or clear the agent when leaving untrusted environments. The SSH server is configured in /etc/ssh/sshd_config and small changes there have outsized security impact. Key recommended settings include disabling PasswordAuthentication after your key-based logins work, setting PermitRootLogin no to block direct root sessions, and using AllowUsers or AllowGroups to limit who can connect. Changing Port from 22 to another number can reduce automated scanning noise, but it is defense by obscurity and not a substitute for proper authentication. After changing sshd_config you must restart the sshd service with sudo systemctl restart sshd for changes to take effect. A concrete example: to require keys only, set PasswordAuthentication no, then keep an active session while testing a key-based login from a new terminal. A frequent mistake is restarting sshd without updating firewall rules to allow the new port; doing this can lock you out. Also check sshd logs via sudo journalctl -u sshd if keys are rejected — logs often give permission or syntax hints. When you make changes, always verify from another connection and keep a recovery plan like console access or a second SSH session. Securing the SSH server (sshd_config) means edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config to disable passwords and root login, restrict users, and always test changes safely before closing your working session.. In practical terms, key settings to reduce risk: disable passwords, root logins, and limit users. Changing the SSH listening port can reduce background scanning noise, but it creates a two‑step operational task: update firewall rules and then update sshd_config. The safe sequence is: open the new port in your firewall first, test connecting to the new port from a separate terminal, and only then restart sshd. For example, open TCP 2222 using your firewall tool, then try ssh -p 2222 user@host from a different console. If the test succeeds, restart sshd and then close the old port. If the test fails, you still have your original session and can revert. A common failure is forgetting to adjust firewall rules, which leads to immediate loss of remote access after restart. Use tools like sudo firewall-cmd --add-port=2222/tcp --permanent and sudo firewall-cmd --reload, or iptables rules depending on your environment. Always leave a recovery path such as console access or an out-of-band console. After the change, update your ~/. ssh/config to include the new port under Host entries so you won't need -p each time. scp provides a familiar copy-like interface to transfer files over an SSH connection. Use scp source destination and scp will securely move data while reusing SSH authentication. For example, to copy a local file to a remote /tmp directory: scp /path/to/local/file. txt username@remote_host_ip:/tmp/. To retrieve a file from a remote host, reverse the order: scp username@remote_host_ip:/path/to/remote/file. txt /path/to/local/. For recursive directory copies use -r. If the server listens on a non‑standard port, include -P 2222 (uppercase P). A common mistake is confusing scp’s -P with ssh’s -p; scp uses -P. Also remember that scp will prompt for a password unless you have key-based authentication or an ssh-agent offering keys. Note that scp uses SSH under the hood, so firewall and authentication considerations are the same. How would you copy an entire project directory to a remote host preserving its structure? sftp opens an interactive file transfer session over SSH and behaves similarly to FTP but within an encrypted channel. Start it with sftp username@remote_host_ip and then use commands like ls, cd, get, and put to navigate and transfer files. This is handy when you want an interactive session to inspect remote directories before copying. For scripted single-file transfers, scp is often quicker. Troubleshooting SSH issues usually follows a short checklist: verify sshd is running with sudo systemctl status sshd, inspect logs with sudo journalctl -u sshd, confirm firewall rules allow the port, and check file permissions on ~/. ssh, authorized_keys (should be 600), and private keys (should be 600 or 400). A common exam-style problem is being prompted for a password despite installing a public key; the likely culprit is improper permissions on the private key or on remote ~/. ssh files. These concise cards capture the essential ideas to retain. SSH is a cryptographic protocol for secure remote access and file transfer; it protects the session and credentials. The sshd daemon runs on the server and enforces authentication and policy as defined in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.
